concepts.name: Composition of the Supreme Court: Strength and Appointment Mechanism
key_dimensions: Constitutional provision (Art. 124) vs. statutory determination of judge strength — Parliament's role in fixing numbers
Current sanctioned strength (34 including CJI) vs. original Constitution provision (8) — evolution via Parliament
Appointment procedure: President's consultation with CJI and other judges — meaning of 'consultation' post-Second Judges Case
UPSC trap: Constitution does NOT fix the number of judges; it only says 'until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number'

concepts.name: Qualifications and Eligibility for Supreme Court Judges
key_dimensions: Art. 124(3): Three routes — HC judge for 5 years, HC advocate for 10 years, distinguished jurist (in President's opinion)
UPSC trap: 'Distinguished jurist' route has never been used in India; compare with UK/US practice
No minimum age prescribed (unlike many countries); retirement age fixed at 65 years under Art. 124(2)
Citizenship requirement: must be a citizen of India — no domicile or birth requirement

concepts.name: Appointment of CJI and the Collegium System
key_dimensions: Art. 124 is silent on seniority convention for CJI appointment — convention vs. constitutional text
First, Second, and Third Judges Cases: evolution from 'consultation' to 'concurrence' to collegium primacy
Collegium composition for SC appointments: CJI + 4 senior-most judges; distinction from HC collegium (CJI + 2)
UPSC trap: NJAC (99th Amendment) struck down in 2015 (Fourth Judges Case) — grounds of judicial independence and basic structure

concepts.name: Removal of Supreme Court Judges: Impeachment Process
key_dimensions: Art. 124(4): Grounds — proved misbehaviour OR incapacity; both Houses must pass address in same session
Special majority required: majority of total membership AND 2/3rd of members present and voting in each House
Judges Inquiry Act 1968: procedure for investigation before address — UPSC trap: investigation precedes the address, not after
Historical fact: No SC judge has been successfully impeached; Justice V. Ramaswami case (1993) — motion failed in Lok Sabha

concepts.name: Independence of the Judiciary: Constitutional Safeguards
key_dimensions: Security of tenure (Art. 124(2)), fixed service conditions (Art. 125), charged expenditure on Consolidated Fund of India
Art. 121 & 217(1): Prohibition on discussion of judges' conduct in Parliament/Legislature except on impeachment motion
Art. 124(7): Prohibition on practice after retirement in courts where they have jurisdiction — UPSC trap: only before SC itself
Contempt of court power as an independence safeguard — Art. 129 (SC) vs. Art. 215 (HC)

concepts.name: Original Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Art. 131)
key_dimensions: Exclusive original jurisdiction in disputes: Centre vs. State(s), State vs. State — UPSC trap: not all inter-state disputes qualify
Exclusion clause: disputes involving private parties, pre-Constitution treaties, or matters under other constitutional provisions (e.g., Art. 262 for inter-state water disputes)
Art. 131 vs. Art. 32: Both give original jurisdiction — Art. 131 is federal; Art. 32 is for FR enforcement
UPSC trap: Art. 131 jurisdiction is EXCLUSIVE — HC cannot hear Centre-State disputes of this nature

concepts.name: Writ Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Art. 32) vs. High Court (Art. 226)
key_dimensions: Art. 32: Right to move SC for enforcement of Fundamental Rights only — itself a Fundamental Right (Part III)
Art. 226: HC can issue writs for FR enforcement AND 'any other purpose' — broader than Art. 32
UPSC trap: SC's writ jurisdiction is narrower in scope (only FRs) but supreme in hierarchy; HC has wider subject matter
Dr. Ambedkar called Art. 32 the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'; Art. 32 cannot be suspended except under Art. 359 (National Emergency)

concepts.name: Appellate Jurisdiction: Constitutional, Civil, and Criminal Appeals
key_dimensions: Constitutional appeals (Art. 132): Any HC judgment involving substantial question of law as to interpretation of Constitution — certificate needed
Civil appeals (Art. 133): Certificate from HC that case involves substantial question of law of general importance — UPSC trap: value of subject matter requirement removed by 30th Amendment
Criminal appeals (Art. 134): Appeal as of right if HC reverses acquittal to death sentence; or sentences to 10+ years; certificate route also available
Art. 136 (Special Leave Petition): Discretionary, residual, extraordinary jurisdiction — can override all other appellate provisions

concepts.name: Special Leave Petition (Art. 136): Scope and Limitations
key_dimensions: Art. 136: SC may grant special leave to appeal from any judgment/decree/order by any court or tribunal in India — except military tribunals (Art. 136(2))
UPSC trap: SLP is discretionary, not a right; SC can refuse without giving reasons
SLP can be filed against interlocutory orders, final orders, or even orders of single HC judges
Distinction: SLP is a pre-appeal stage; once granted, it becomes a regular appeal — different procedural consequences

concepts.name: Advisory Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Art. 143)
key_dimensions: President can seek SC opinion on questions of law or fact of public importance — SC's opinion is NOT binding on President
Two categories: (1) May refer — SC may refuse to answer; (2) Pre-Constitution treaties/agreements — SC MUST give opinion (UPSC trap on this distinction)
SC has exercised discretion to decline opinions (e.g., Ayodhya reference 1993 — SC declined as it involved disputed facts)
Advisory opinion ≠ judicial decision — not binding as precedent; compare with USA where SC has no advisory jurisdiction

concepts.name: Law of the Land: Art. 141 and Binding Nature of SC Decisions
key_dimensions: Art. 141: Law declared by SC shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India — includes ratio decidendi, not obiter dicta
UPSC trap: Art. 141 binds all 'courts' — question of whether it binds tribunals (held: yes, by SC itself in various cases)
SC is NOT bound by its own decisions but can overrule them (larger bench principle) — distinguish from HC which is bound by SC
Prospective overruling doctrine (Golak Nath case) — SC can declare a decision applicable only for future cases

concepts.name: Review Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (Art. 137)
key_dimensions: Art. 137: SC has power to review its own judgments — subject to provisions of law made by Parliament and rules under Art. 145
Grounds for review: error apparent on face of record, new evidence, or sufficient reason — NOT a rehearing on merits
UPSC trap: Review petition is heard by the same bench (usually in chambers without oral arguments) — distinguish from Curative Petition
Curative Petition (Rupa Ashok Hurra case, 2002): Post-review remedy; heard by 3 senior-most judges + bench that decided review — very rare remedy

concepts.name: Court of Record Status and Contempt Powers (Art. 129)
key_dimensions: Art. 129: SC is a court of record — records have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned in any court
Inherent power to punish for contempt of itself — civil contempt vs. criminal contempt distinction
Contempt of Courts Act 1971: Defines and limits contempt; 'truth' as a defence added by 2006 amendment — UPSC trap on this amendment
Art. 215 gives same court of record status to HCs — UPSC trap: both SC and HC are courts of record, but SC's contempt power is supreme

concepts.name: Transfer of Cases and Judges: Arts. 139A and 222
key_dimensions: Art. 139A: SC can transfer cases involving same/substantial questions of law from one HC to another or to itself
UPSC trap: Transfer under Art. 139A is on SC's own motion OR on application of Attorney General or a party
Art. 222: President (after consultation with CJI) can transfer HC judges — CJI's concurrence is effectively required post-Third Judges Case
Distinction: Art. 139A transfers CASES; Art. 222 transfers JUDGES — frequently confused in UPSC questions

concepts.name: Seat of the Supreme Court and Bench Sittings
key_dimensions: Art. 130: SC shall sit in Delhi OR such other place(s) as CJI may appoint with approval of President — CJI has discretion
UPSC trap: Constitution does NOT permanently fix Delhi; CJI can designate circuit benches — demand for regional SC benches is a recurring debate
Constitutional Bench: Matters involving substantial constitutional questions must be heard by minimum 5 judges (Art. 145(3))
Quorum for SC sittings: Minimum 3 judges (Art. 145(2) read with Supreme Court Rules) — UPSC trap: quorum ≠ constitutional bench strength

concepts.name: Jurisdiction Over Fundamental Rights: Art. 32 as a Fundamental Right Itself
key_dimensions: Art. 32 is in Part III — the right to move SC is itself a guaranteed FR, not merely a procedural remedy
Art. 32 can be suspended during National Emergency under Art. 359 — UPSC trap: Art. 20 and 21 FRs CANNOT be suspended even under Art. 359 (44th Amendment)
Distinction between Art. 32 (SC only, FRs only) and Art. 226 (HC, FRs + other legal rights) — PIL development under Art. 32
Locus standi liberalisation under Art. 32: PIL allows any public-spirited person to approach SC — judicial innovation, not constitutional text

concepts.name: Ad Hoc Judges and Acting CJI Appointments
key_dimensions: Art. 127: CJI can appoint ad hoc judges from HC (with consent of HC CJ and President) when SC quorum cannot be maintained
Art. 128: Retired SC judges can be requested by CJI (with President's approval) to sit and act as SC judges
UPSC trap: Art. 127 = ad hoc from HC; Art. 128 = retired SC judges — both are different provisions often confused
Art. 126: President appoints Acting CJI when CJI office is vacant or CJI is absent — not the next senior judge automatically by constitutional text

concepts.name: Doctrine of Judicial Review: Constitutional Basis and Scope
key_dimensions: Not explicitly mentioned in Constitution but derived from Arts. 13, 32, 131, 132, 133, 134, 136, 143, 226, 227
Art. 13: Laws inconsistent with FRs are void — primary textual basis for judicial review of legislation
Scope: Judicial review of legislative action, executive action, and constitutional amendments (post-Kesavananda Bharati)
UPSC trap: India follows 'limited' judicial review (can strike down laws) unlike USA's broader model; but India cannot review political questions (doctrine of non-justiciability)

concepts.name: Separation of Powers and Judicial Overreach: Constitutional Boundaries
key_dimensions: India follows functional separation, not strict separation — SC can issue directions to executive under Art. 32/142
Art. 142: SC can pass any order necessary for doing 'complete justice' — extraordinary and unique power with no HC equivalent
UPSC trap: Art. 142 is frequently debated as judicial overreach vs. judicial activism — Vineet Narain case, Vishaka case as examples
Distinction between judicial activism (filling legislative vacuum) and judicial overreach (encroaching on executive/legislative domain) — recurring Mains theme

concepts.name: Inter-State Water Disputes and Exclusion from SC's Original Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Art. 262: Parliament can exclude SC jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes — exception to Art. 131's general federal jurisdiction
Inter-State Water Disputes Act 1956: Establishes tribunals; SC cannot entertain such disputes if tribunal is set up — UPSC trap on this exclusion
Once a tribunal gives award, it has same force as SC decree — but SC cannot be approached directly bypassing the tribunal
Contrast: For all other Centre-State/State-State disputes, Art. 131 gives SC EXCLUSIVE jurisdiction — water disputes are the KEY EXCEPTION
